Is there a separate Georgia tax on profit from selling a house?

No. Georgia does not tax capital gains differently than other income, so your gain goes on the regular state income tax return. The state's flat income tax rate is 4.99%, with standard deductions of $15,000 for single filers, heads of household and married people filing separately, and $30,000 for joint filers. Questions the forms do not answer go to the Department of Revenue's Taxpayer Services Division.

In practice the federal return does most of the sorting. If the IRS lets you exclude the profit on a main home, the amount that reaches Georgia is small or zero.

The federal home sale exclusion

Usually the exclusion carries over to the state return. Georgia's withholding rules for nonresident sellers treat gain excluded from federal adjusted gross income as exempt, which tells you the state follows the federal treatment of a main residence.

The federal exclusion tops out at $250,000 of gain for one filer or $500,000 on a joint return. To qualify you need two things inside the five years before closing: 24 months of ownership and 24 months of living in the house. Spouses on a joint return both need the living requirement, and a prior exclusion within the last two years can block a new one.

Publication 523 holds the worksheets. Military and some foreign service households can pause the five-year clock for as long as 10 years.

How leftover gain is measured and taxed federally

Gain equals what you realized minus adjusted basis. Basis starts with your cost and rises with value-adding improvements, then falls with depreciation or insurance payments for casualty losses.

For tax years beginning in 2025, most net capital gain is taxed at no more than 15% for most people, with a 0% bracket at lower incomes. A 20% rate applies above the 15% limits. A rented, depreciated house can pull in a 25% maximum rate on the unrecaptured section 1250 portion. A loss on a personal home cannot be deducted.

Single$48,350$533,400

Head of household$64,750$566,700
Married filing separately$48,350$300,000

Withholding at the closing table

Nonresident sellers have tax withheld. Under O.C.G.A. 48-7-128 the buyer holds back 3% of the price and sends it to the state, and the seller later claims credit on a Georgia return. Several exits exist:

  • A main home that qualifies under federal law is exempt for the gain federal law excludes.
  • A sworn gain affidavit, Form IT-AFF2, lets withholding drop to 3% of the gain.
  • Prices under $20,000 are exempt, and so are sales where the tax comes to less than $600 and the seller signs the affidavit.
  • A nonresident who meets every statutory condition can sign a deemed-resident affidavit.
  • Only net proceeds are withheld when 3% exceeds the cash due to the seller.

The buyer must send the money in by the last day of the month after closing. A buyer who skips withholding can end up personally liable, so the closing office will ask about your residency early.

Papers to gather before the gain is figured

Receipts shrink gains. Improvements add to basis, and the amount realized is figured after selling costs, so an organized folder can lower the number you report.

  • The settlement statement from your purchase.
  • Invoices for work that added value, such as a new addition or a finished room.
  • Records of depreciation, casualty reimbursements or rental use.
  • Proof of where you lived and when, such as utility bills, to show the 24-month use test.
  • The final settlement statement from this sale, and a Form 1099-S if one arrives.

Heirs and gift recipients follow separate basis rules found in Publication 551. Have a tax preparer confirm basis before you price the house.

Estimated tax after a profitable sale

You may owe it. Anyone with a taxable capital gain may be required to make estimated tax payments, and Publication 505 has the test. A large gain landing in a single quarter is the usual trigger, so raise it with a preparer before closing.

People with significant investment income may also owe the net investment income tax, covered in IRS Topic no. 559. That is a federal layer on top of the rates in the table above.

A sale closed in a given calendar year is reported on the return filed the following spring. Set aside money from the proceeds for both the federal and Georgia returns before you spend the cash.

  • Ask whether your withholding or estimates already cover the gain.
  • Keep the withholding statement if the buyer held back 3% for Georgia.
  • Match the figures on your return to the final settlement statement.

Reporting a Georgia house sale to the IRS

Report the sale whenever a Form 1099-S shows up, even if the entire profit is excludable. Report it as well when part of the profit exceeds the exclusion. Schedule D and Form 8949 are the forms for the job.

The 1099-S is built from the settlement statement, so compare the sale price and the seller name on the statement with your own records. Ask the closing office to fix any mismatch before the form is filed.

Older sellers and installment sales

Georgia gives taxpayers 62 or older, and those permanently and totally disabled, a retirement income adjustment. Capital gains income counts as qualifying retirement income alongside pensions, interest, dividends and net rental income. The Form IT-511 booklet gives the yearly cap.

A sale paid out over several years is an installment sale. You report gain as payments arrive unless you elect out by the return's due date, interest counts as ordinary income, and the home exclusion stays available.

Why the sale price and net proceeds differ at closing

Tax is only one reason the check you receive is smaller than the contract price. Seller costs, the mortgage payoff and any county tax bill come off first, and withholding for a nonresident comes out of whatever cash is due to you.

That is why a draft settlement statement is worth requesting a few days before closing. Compare the sale price on it with your own figures, confirm whether Georgia withholding applies, and ask the closing office what paperwork it needs from you. A cash buyer skips the lender's underwriting, but the same statement and the same tax forms still apply.

Frequently asked questions

What rate applies to capital gains in Georgia?

Georgia has no capital gains rate of its own. Gains are taxed like other income at the flat income tax rate of 4.99%.

How much profit on my Georgia house can I keep tax free?

Up to $250,000 as one filer or $500,000 on a joint return, when you meet the 24-month ownership and use tests. Publication 523 on irs.gov has the worksheets and the exceptions.

Does an out-of-state owner face withholding on a Georgia sale?

Often yes. The buyer withholds 3% of the price, or 3% of the gain with a sworn affidavit, unless an exemption applies. A qualifying main home is exempt for excluded gain, and prices under $20,000 are exempt.

Do I report the sale if no tax is due?

Yes when you get a Form 1099-S or when some gain cannot be excluded. Schedule D and Form 8949 are the forms for that reporting.

What basis do I use for an inherited Georgia house?

Inherited property follows its own basis rules, covered in Publication 551. Have a tax preparer confirm the figure before you set a price.

How a Georgia tax sale works

A Georgia tax sale is a public auction of a delinquent property after a tax lien has been issued and the property has been advertised. The winning bidder receives a tax deed, and the owner keeps a right to buy the property back. Sales run under O.C.G.A. 48-3-1 and 48-4-1 and following.

The county sets the calendar. DeKalb holds sales on the first Tuesday of the month from April through December on the courthouse steps in Decatur. Cobb holds them on the first Tuesday of the months it plans a sale, moving to Wednesday if Tuesday is a holiday. Gwinnett generally holds sales in only a few selected months.

Opening bids are the unpaid taxes plus penalties, interest, and costs. Georgia sells the deed, and the lien itself is not what changes hands. Cobb is explicit that it sells tax deeds and does not sell tax liens.

Sale day for bidders

Registration comes first. Cobb requires pre-registration for each sale and issues bidder cards between 9:00 and 10:00 a.m. on the day, against a photo ID. DeKalb requires registration for each sale as well, either online beforehand or in person that morning.

  • Payment. Cobb wants payment in full when the sale ends, by cash or certified check. DeKalb requires cash, a cashier's check or a certified check from an insured institution within one hour after the sale ends.
  • Failure to pay. In DeKalb an unpaid bid goes back up for resale the same afternoon, and the defaulting bidder may owe the difference or be barred from later sales.
  • Unsold parcels. Cobb may re-auction properties that drew no bid at 3 p.m. that afternoon.
  • Buyer beware. The doctrine of caveat emptor applies to every tax sale.

For an owner, the same details matter in reverse: once a sale is scheduled, DeKalb accepts only cash, bank cashier's checks or bank wires, and Gwinnett accepts only certified funds.

How long the owner can take the property back

At least 12 months, and often longer. O.C.G.A. 48-4-40 lets the defendant in the execution, or anyone with a right, title, interest or lien in the property, redeem within 12 months of the sale, and after that until the right is cut off by the statutory notice.

The redemption price is set by 48-4-42, for sales after July 1, 2002. These are its pieces.

What the redemption payment includes
ComponentRule
BidThe amount paid at the tax sale, as shown in the tax deed
Later taxesAny taxes the purchaser paid after the sale
Special assessmentsAny special assessments on the property
Premium20 percent for the first year or fraction of a year since the sale, then 10 percent for each additional year or fraction of a year
Notice costsSheriff's cost for serving the notice and publication costs, if redemption comes more than 30 days after the foreclosure notice
Association sumsFor sales after July 1, 2016, certain amounts paid to a property owners', condominium or homeowners' association

Payment goes to the purchaser in lawful United States money. In Cobb the tax sale purchaser works out the redemption amount, so ask the purchaser or the tax commissioner for a written figure.

Can the purchaser move in after the sale?

No. In Cobb, the purchaser gets a tax deed but cannot take possession, make improvements, evict tenants or move onto the property. In Gwinnett, buyers at a sale do not automatically own the property and owners are not immediately evicted.

The purchaser can end the owner's right to redeem only by following the notice rules in 48-4-45. After 12 months the purchaser serves notice on the defendant in the execution, the occupant, and everyone with a recorded interest or lien in the county, and must publish it once a week for four consecutive weeks in the sheriff's advertisement newspaper. Notice to people outside the county goes by registered or certified mail or statutory overnight delivery.

Even then the deed is not final overnight. Under 48-4-48 a tax deed executed at a valid sale after July 1, 1996 ripens into fee simple title four years after the deed is recorded in the county land records.

Redemption and extra sale money

Redemption puts the title back in the owner, subject to every lien that existed at the time of the sale (48-4-43). The purchaser must then sign a quitclaim deed to the owner under 48-4-44, naming who paid the redemption money. If it is not presented at redemption, the purchaser has seven days to supply one properly witnessed, and it must reach the clerk of the superior court within ten days of the redemption. Our quitclaim deed guide explains that kind of deed.

When a sale brings in more than taxes and costs, the extra money belongs to the parties with an interest. Cobb's tax commissioner may file an interpleader in superior court to distribute it, and DeKalb holds excess funds until a rightful party files a claim. DeKalb accepts claims only from the entitled party or a Georgia attorney, and not from an agent under a power of attorney.

The court-supervised sale

Counties and cities that adopt the process under 48-4-76 can foreclose through superior court instead. The sale is advertised as sheriffs' sales are, cannot occur earlier than 45 days after the court's order, and the minimum bid is the redemption amount.

The owner's redemption window is shorter, 60 days after the sale, and the owner redeems by paying the minimum bid price into the superior court. Within 90 days after the sale, the petitioner must deliver the deed and file a report of the sale. Any surplus above the minimum bid is deposited with the court and distributed by priority to the interested parties, including the owner.

Selling your house before a tax sale

Yes, a sale to a buyer that closes before the auction can pay the delinquent taxes out of the proceeds. Payment of everything owed stops the sale, and in Gwinnett the owner can pay all taxes, costs and fees after a property is selected for sale, in certified funds. Ask the tax commissioner for a payoff figure through your closing date, since advertising and title research fees keep being added as the sale approaches.

If the auction has already taken place, the 12 month redemption period is the next deadline. A buyer purchasing from you then has to account for the purchaser's rights as well, so involve a Georgia real estate attorney and a title company early.

Bring the delinquent tax notice, your deed and a recent payoff letter to the title company. A cash sale skips lender underwriting, which can help when the sale date is close.

Frequently asked questions

Where are Georgia tax sales held?

At the county, usually at the courthouse. DeKalb holds them on the courthouse steps in Decatur, Cobb at the Superior Court Plaza, and Gwinnett in front of the Justice and Administration Center in Lawrenceville.

How long do I have to redeem after a Georgia tax sale?

At least 12 months from the sale date. After that the right continues until the purchaser cuts it off by giving the statutory foreclosure notice to the owner, the occupant and recorded interest holders.

What does redemption cost?

The purchaser's bid, plus later taxes the purchaser paid, special assessments, and a premium of 20 percent for the first year or fraction and 10 percent for each additional year or fraction. Notice costs may be added. Get the exact figure in writing.

Does the buyer at a tax sale own the house immediately?

No. The buyer holds a tax deed that works like a lien until redemption rights end. In Cobb the purchaser cannot take possession, improve the property or evict tenants during that time.

What happens to extra money from a tax sale?

It is held for the parties entitled to it. DeKalb takes claims from the entitled party or a Georgia attorney, and Cobb may file an interpleader action in superior court to distribute the money.
